title: Budgeting
examples: What is the best way to start budgeting for a new job?
Can the 50/30/20 rule change if I have student loans?
How often should I review my budget to stay on track?

explain.say: Today we learn a helpful budgeting model called fifty thirty twenty.
The first part is needs which should take up about fifty percent of your income.
Next we look at wants which should not exceed thirty percent of your total income.
Finally savings and debt repayment should take up the remaining twenty percent of your pay.
A real life example is tracking your monthly spending for one full month.
A common mistake is forgetting to track small daily purchases like coffee or snacks.

faq.q: Does the 50/30/20 rule work for everyone?
faq.a: No, it is a guideline, not a strict law for everyone. Your situation, like location or family size, might require adjustments. You might also ask: Is this rule flexible? How do I adjust this rule for my income?
asks: What if my rent is too high for 50%?

faq.q: What should I do if my needs are over 50 percent?
faq.a: If needs exceed fifty percent, you may need to look at reducing those costs, perhaps by finding cheaper housing or cutting utility usage. You could also ask: Can I afford to live somewhere that costs too much? What if I have high necessary expenses?
asks: My housing costs are too high.
How do I cut down on essential bills?

faq.q: Does 'wants' mean I can't have any fun money?
faq.a: No, 'wants' simply means non-essential spending like eating out or hobbies. It is about balance, so you must allocate some money for enjoyment. You might also ask: Is 'fun money' always a want? Can I cut back on wants temporarily?
asks: What is the difference between a want and a need?
Can I save money by cutting out all entertainment?

faq.q: How do I actually track my spending effectively?
faq.a: You can use budgeting apps, keep a dedicated notebook, or review your bank statements regularly for accuracy. Consistency is the most important part of tracking. You might ask: What tools should I use for tracking? Is tracking hard to maintain?
asks: What is the easiest way to track expenses?
Should I track with paper or an app?

faq.q: Does this rule change if I get a raise or a bonus?
faq.a: Yes, when your income increases, you should aim to allocate the extra money according to the same percentages, prioritizing savings first. You can also ask: How should I handle unexpected income? Should I save all my bonuses?
asks: What if my income increases next month?
How do I budget for a raise?

facts: Needs are expenses required for basic survival, like housing and food.
Wants are non-essential expenses that improve quality of life, like dining out.
Savings and debt repayment should be treated as a non-negotiable expense.
Tracking spending requires recording every single transaction for accuracy.

quiz.say: If your rent takes up 60 percent of your income, which category is most affected?
quiz.why: The 50 percent guideline for needs is exceeded, indicating a potential imbalance in essential spending.

wrong.0: Wants are flexible and should absorb the excess spending, but this is not the first place to look.
wrong.1: Savings should remain protected; they are for future goals, not to cover overspending in needs.
wrong.2: Debt payments are part of the 20 percent, but the issue here is the initial overspending in needs.

quiz.say: You spend twenty dollars on lunch and twenty dollars on a movie ticket. Which category do these fall into?
quiz.why: Both lunch and movies are discretionary spending, meaning they are wants rather than absolute necessities.

wrong.0: Spending money on current activities does not count towards future savings goals.
wrong.1: This is spending money, not money used to pay back a loan or debt.
wrong.3: These items are enjoyable extras, not things required just to stay alive.

quiz.say: If you track all your spending and find your actual spending is 60 percent needs, 25 percent wants, and 15 percent savings, what is the most important action to take next?

options.show: Reduce spending in the Needs category.
options.say: Reduce spending in the Needs category.

quiz.why: Since needs are over the 50 percent limit, the immediate focus must be on reducing the largest expense area.

wrong.1: Increasing wants when needs are already too high will make the budget worse.
wrong.2: Cutting savings when needs are over budget makes the problem worse by ignoring future security.
wrong.3: Ignoring the numbers means you will not know how to fix the spending pattern.
